topic: Sound for Picture — Post Workflow & Deliverables

fields.definition: In Foley, the practice of performing and editing hand-related sounds — grabs, pats, claps and prop contacts — so they line up precisely, frame by frame, with the actor's hand movements on screen.
fields.plain_english: It means making the sound of hands match what the hands do on screen. If the actor claps, the clap sound must land at the exact same moment.
fields.purpose_function: It restores believable, sync-accurate hand sounds that the production microphone missed or captured poorly, keeping what the audience sees and hears in agreement.
fields.practical_application: A Foley artist loops the picture and re-performs each hand action to a monitor, then the Foley editor nudges the takes in the DAW until every contact hits its frame.
common_mistakes: Treating rough sync as good enough — hand sounds even a frame or two off read as fake to the audience.
Performing the motion without watching the picture, so the rhythm of the sounds drifts from the on-screen action.
Doubling hand sounds that already exist in usable production audio.
scenario_contexts: Adding clap and handshake sounds to a dialogue scene shot on a noisy location.
Re-syncing hand pats and applause for a crowd insert.
Matching prop-handling hand contacts in an ADR-heavy scene where production audio was discarded.

sources: Vanessa Theme Ament, The Foley Grail: The Art of Performing Sound for Film, Games, and Animation (Focal Press)
David Lewis Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound (Focal Press)

fields.definition: A dedicated listening space used to audition a finished mix over reference headphones, confirming that its balance, dialogue clarity and spatial imaging translate for the large audience that listens on headphones and earbuds.
fields.plain_english: It is a room set up to check how a mix sounds through headphones. Many people watch shows with earbuds, so mixers make sure it still sounds right there.
fields.purpose_function: It exists because a mix balanced on room monitors can shift on headphones, so a controlled headphone check protects dialogue and spatial cues for headphone listeners.
fields.practical_application: A re-recording mixer takes a near-final mix into this space, plays it on calibrated headphones, and flags any dialogue, bass or panning that only works on the main monitors.
common_mistakes: Assuming a mix that sounds great on studio monitors will automatically translate to headphones.
Judging headphone translation on random consumer earbuds instead of a known reference set.
Monitoring too loud on headphones, which hides balance problems that appear at normal listening levels.
scenario_contexts: Checking a streaming series mix that most viewers will hear on earbuds.
Confirming a binaural or immersive headphone render before delivery.
Spotting a boosted low end that only becomes obvious on closed-back headphones.

sources: Bobby Owsinski, The Mixing Engineer's Handbook (translation across playback systems)
Tomlinson Holman, Sound for Film and Television (Focal Press) — monitoring and translation

fields.definition: A game parameter (real-time parameter control) that reports a character's or object's remaining health to the audio engine, letting the game's sound change continuously as that health value rises or falls.
fields.plain_english: It is a number from the game that tells the sound system how healthy a character is. As health drops, the audio can change, like a heartbeat that gets louder when you are hurt.
fields.purpose_function: It links game state to sound so audio can react to health in real time — muffling the mix, adding a heartbeat, or shifting the music when a player nears death.
fields.practical_application: A game-audio implementer maps the health parameter to a low-pass filter and a heartbeat loop in Wwise or FMOD, so the mix darkens and the pulse rises as health falls toward zero.
common_mistakes: Confusing the health parameter (a game value) with the audio effects it drives, such as the heartbeat itself.
Mapping health to sound with an abrupt curve, so the audio jumps instead of changing smoothly.
Updating the parameter too infrequently, causing audible stepping as health changes.
scenario_contexts: Adding a rising heartbeat as a player's health drops in a shooter.
Muffling and desaturating the mix during a low-health near-death state.
Switching music intensity when a boss's health crosses a threshold.

sources: Audiokinetic Wwise documentation — Game Parameters (RTPC), Wwise-101 Lesson 3
Richard Stevens & Dave Raybould, Game Audio Implementation / The Game Audio Tutorial (Focal Press)

fields.definition: A game-audio system that generates collision and impact sounds at runtime by taking physics data — such as material type, velocity and mass — and selecting or shaping the appropriate hit, thud or crash.
fields.plain_english: It is a set-up that makes crash and bump sounds by itself when things collide in a game. It picks the right sound based on what hit what and how hard.
fields.purpose_function: It exists so that unpredictable, physics-driven collisions still produce believable, varied impact sounds without a sound designer hand-placing every hit.
fields.practical_application: An implementer connects the physics engine's collision events to sound containers keyed by material and velocity, so a light tap and a heavy crash draw from different samples.
common_mistakes: Triggering one impact sound regardless of velocity, so gentle and violent hits sound identical.
Not limiting simultaneous impacts, so a pile-up of collisions creates a harsh, distorted burst.
Ignoring material data, so a metal-on-stone hit plays a wood sound.
scenario_contexts: Generating debris and impact sounds as a physics-driven structure collapses.
Playing correct hit sounds when objects of different materials collide in a sandbox game.
Scaling impact loudness with collision force in a racing or combat title.

sources: Audiokinetic Wwise documentation — containers and event triggering; Firelight FMOD Studio documentation
Richard Stevens & Dave Raybould, Game Audio Implementation (Focal Press)

fields.definition: A container in game-audio middleware that holds several child sounds and plays them together as simultaneous layers, so a single event outputs a blended, composite sound rather than one file.
fields.plain_english: It is a holder that plays several sounds at once, stacked on top of each other. It is like layering a few tracks so they blend into one bigger sound.
fields.purpose_function: It lets designers build one rich sound from stacked elements — such as a low rumble, a mid body and a high detail — and control or crossfade those layers together.
fields.practical_application: A designer drops the sub, body and detail layers of an explosion into a layer container so they always trigger together and can be blended with one game parameter.
common_mistakes: Confusing a layer container (plays sounds together) with a sequence or random container (plays sounds one at a time).
Stacking too many layers, wasting voices and muddying the sound.
Leaving layers phase-misaligned, so combining them thins the sound instead of thickening it.
scenario_contexts: Building a layered weapon or explosion sound from separate low, mid and high elements.
Crossfading engine layers with RPM using one game parameter.
Combining a base ambience with intermittent detail layers for a location.

sources: Audiokinetic Wwise documentation — Blend Container (summing and layering with Blend Containers)
Richard Stevens & Dave Raybould, Game Audio Implementation (Focal Press)

fields.definition: A transitional sound-design element built largely from filtered or swept noise — such as a riser, whoosh or sweep — used to bridge two scenes, shots or sections and carry the ear across the cut.
fields.plain_english: It is a whoosh or sweep sound made from noise that carries the viewer from one scene to the next. It smooths over the jump between shots.
fields.purpose_function: It smooths and energises edits by giving the audience an audible bridge across a picture change, hiding the seam and building or releasing tension.
fields.practical_application: An editor places a rising noise sweep a few frames before a hard cut so its peak lands on the new shot, gluing the transition together.
common_mistakes: Making the transition so loud it overwhelms the dialogue or music around the cut.
Peaking the sweep at the wrong moment, so it fights rather than supports the picture change.
Overusing noise whooshes until every edit sounds the same.
scenario_contexts: Bridging a flashback with a filtered noise sweep in a trailer.
Whooshing between locations in a fast montage.
Adding a riser into a reveal or title card.

sources: David Sonnenschein, Sound Design: The Expressive Power of Music, Voice and Sound Effects in Cinema (Michael Wiese)
Ric Viers, The Sound Effects Bible (Michael Wiese Productions)

fields.definition: A Foley or sound-effect element covering the sound of a character picking up or setting down a handled object — the contact, grip and material movement of the prop as it leaves or meets a surface.
fields.plain_english: It is the sound of someone picking something up or putting it down. Think of the small clink and rustle when a hand grabs a cup off a table.
fields.purpose_function: It adds tactile realism to on-screen handling, telling the audience an object has weight and material even when the production mic missed the contact.
fields.practical_application: A Foley artist handles a matching prop in sync with the picture, capturing the pick-up and set-down contacts that the editor then places to frame.
common_mistakes: Using a generic clink for every object instead of matching the prop's real material and weight.
Placing the pick-up sound off the frame where the hand actually grips the object.
Forgetting the set-down sound, so objects seem to vanish rather than be placed.
scenario_contexts: Adding the sound of a character picking up a coffee mug.
Covering a character lifting and holstering a prop weapon.
Selling the weight of a heavy box as it is lifted off the floor.

sources: Vanessa Theme Ament, The Foley Grail (Focal Press)
Ric Viers, The Sound Effects Bible (Michael Wiese Productions)

fields.definition: A Foley category covering the sounds of manipulating paper materials — rustling, folding, crumpling, sorting and page movement — performed to match on-screen handling of documents, books, letters or packaging.
fields.plain_english: It is the rustle and crinkle sound of someone handling paper. Like the noise a letter makes when it is unfolded or a stack of pages is shuffled.
fields.purpose_function: It gives paper actions audible texture and weight, making documents, books and letters feel real and reinforcing the pace of the on-screen handling.
fields.practical_application: A Foley artist rustles and folds matching paper stock in sync with the picture, choosing weight and stiffness to suit the document shown.
common_mistakes: Using the wrong paper weight, so a thin note sounds like heavy cardstock.
Over-performing rustles until routine handling sounds distractingly busy.
Letting the paper sound drift off sync with the visible page or fold.
scenario_contexts: Covering a character reading and folding a letter.
Adding page rustles as someone flips through a report.
Selling the handling of a newspaper or map in a dialogue scene.

sources: Vanessa Theme Ament, The Foley Grail (Focal Press)
David Lewis Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound (Focal Press)

fields.definition: A Foley movement category covering the crinkle, creak and rustle of plastic materials — bags, packaging, rain gear, tarps and hard plastic props — performed to match on-screen handling or body movement.
fields.plain_english: It is the crinkle and creak sound of plastic being moved. Like the noise a shopping bag or a raincoat makes when someone shifts around.
fields.purpose_function: It adds material-specific texture to movement, distinguishing plastic from cloth or leather and reinforcing what a character is wearing or handling.
fields.practical_application: A Foley artist manipulates matching plastic — a bag, a tarp or a raincoat — in sync with the actor, layering it under footsteps or handling as needed.
common_mistakes: Choosing plastic with the wrong stiffness, so soft film sounds like a rigid crate.
Performing plastic crinkle louder than the scene warrants, pulling focus from dialogue.
Reusing the same plastic rustle for every material instead of matching the prop.
scenario_contexts: Adding raincoat crinkle to a character walking in a storm.
Covering the handling of a plastic shopping bag.
Layering tarp movement over a construction-site scene.

sources: Vanessa Theme Ament, The Foley Grail (Focal Press)
Ric Viers, The Sound Effects Bible (Michael Wiese Productions)

fields.definition: A Foley movement element covering the sound of a hand entering or leaving a pocket and its contents shifting inside — fabric friction plus the muted rattle of keys, coins or a phone.
fields.plain_english: It is the sound of a hand going into a pocket and the stuff inside moving. Like the soft jingle and rustle when someone reaches for their keys.
fields.purpose_function: It adds a small but telling layer of realism to a character's movement and business, cueing the audience that something is being reached for or stowed.
fields.practical_application: A Foley artist performs the reach into a matching garment pocket, adding coin or key content to sync with the actor's hand action.
common_mistakes: Adding a loud coin rattle when the character's pocket should be empty.
Letting the pocket sound sit off sync with the visible hand movement.
Using the same content rattle regardless of what the character carries.
scenario_contexts: Covering a character reaching for keys or a phone.
Adding fabric and content movement as someone pockets an object.
Layering pocket business under a walking shot to build character.

sources: Vanessa Theme Ament, The Foley Grail (Focal Press)
David Lewis Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound (Focal Press)

fields.definition: A randomized playback mode in which a container or playlist selects its child sounds in random order but does not repeat any element until all have played, avoiding immediate repetition while still varying the sequence.
fields.plain_english: It is a random play mode that mixes up the order of sounds but will not repeat one until all have played. It works like shuffling a deck of cards before dealing.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to keep repeated sounds — footsteps, gunshots, impacts — from sounding mechanically identical while still ensuring every variation is used before any repeats.
fields.practical_application: An implementer sets a random container of footstep variations to shuffle so consecutive steps never reuse the same sample, reducing the machine-gun effect.
common_mistakes: Confusing shuffle (no repeat until all have played) with pure random, which can repeat the same sound back-to-back.
Loading too few variations, so even shuffled playback becomes obvious.
Assuming shuffle randomizes pitch or volume — it only randomizes selection order.
scenario_contexts: Varying footstep samples so a character's walk never machine-guns.
Cycling weapon-fire variations during sustained shooting.
Playing ambient one-shots like bird calls in a non-repeating random order.

sources: Audiokinetic Wwise documentation — Random Container play modes (Standard vs Shuffle)
Firelight Technologies FMOD Studio documentation — Multi Instrument playlist / shuffle
